item.text: I’m adding only distinct remembered omissions—especially the negative communal counterexamples, reconciliation continuations, and Jewish friendship and dispute traditions. I’ll save the TSV without reading it back.

item.command:
/bin/bash -lc "cat > /Volumes/aro/projects/prose_generation/enrichment/bible/work/s103/discovery/s103-20261009/sec9/luna/followup.tsv <<'EOF'
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Lev.19.18	neighbor-love instead of vengeance or grudge	The verse forbids vengeance and resentment between members of the people before commanding love of neighbor; it gives the commentary's move from conflict to closeness a concrete ethical form.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Zech.7.9	true judgments joined to kindness and mercy	Zechariah tells the community to judge truthfully and show compassion to one another; this adds mercy to the commentary's link between haqq and peace.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Zech.8.17	do not scheme evil against one another	The verse forbids plotting harm against a neighbor and loving false oaths; it continues the preceding truth-and-peace formula with an explicit interpersonal restraint.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Mal.2.10	one Father and treachery between brothers	Malachi asks why people betray one another if they share one creator and ancestral covenant; this grounds the commentary's kinship bond in a moral claim against division.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Prov.12.15	wise person listens to counsel	The fool thinks his way right in his own eyes, but the wise listen to counsel; this directly answers the commentary's image of each side claiming haqq for itself.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Prov.15.18	slow anger calms contention	The patient person quiets a quarrel, while the hot-tempered one stirs it; this gives sabr a direct social effect in ending strife.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Prov.17.9	repeating an offense separates close friends	The proverb says covering a transgression seeks love while repeating it divides intimate friends; it makes the commentary's friend-bond vulnerable to speech that renews conflict.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Prov.25.15	patience persuades and a gentle tongue prevails	The proverb joins patience and gentle speech in persuading a ruler; it adds a specific way counsel can change a hard position without quarrel.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Prov.25.21	feed an enemy who is hungry	The proverb commands concrete care for an enemy in need; it gives an action by which the commentary's transition from enmity toward friendship can begin.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Prov.27.6	faithful wounds from a friend	The proverb treats a friend's painful rebuke as faithful; it clarifies that the commentary's mutual advice can correct rather than merely affirm a companion.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Ps.120.8	peace offered but met with war	The speaker says he is for peace while those around him want war; this preserves a counter-case to the commentary's hopeful passage from mutual speech to peace.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Ps.122.9	peace wished for brothers and companions	The pilgrim's formula wishes peace within Jerusalem for the sake of brothers and companions; it joins liturgical speech, friendship, and communal peace in one line.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Job.19.13	brothers and acquaintances estranged from Job	Job says his kin have withdrawn and his acquaintances are strangers; this gives a stark counter-image to the commentary's claim that human loss is answered by bonds.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Job.19.19	intimate friends turn against Job	Job says those he loved have turned against him; this preserves the contrary reading that close friendship can collapse into aversion.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Gen.45.5	Joseph tells frightened brothers not to grieve over their betrayal	Joseph reframes their sale of him as God's means of preserving life; the speech releases his brothers from fear and turns a contested wrong toward reconciliation.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Gen.50.21	Joseph comforts his brothers and speaks kindly	After the brothers fear revenge again, Joseph reassures and comforts them; this is a necessary continuation showing reconciliation maintained through compassionate speech.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:1Sam.25.33	Abigail's counsel keeps David from bloodguilt	David blesses Abigail for restraining him from revenge; her wise intervention makes counsel the means by which a violent conflict is prevented.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:1Kgs.12.7	elders advise the king to serve and answer gently	The elders tell Rehoboam that serving the people and speaking good words will win their service; this makes reciprocal regard a practical alternative to coercive rule.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:1Kgs.12.16	rejected counsel ends in the people's division	After Rehoboam rejects the elders' advice, Israel refuses his rule and separates; this shows the social loss that follows counsel answered with hardness.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Gen.11.3	people speak to one another to build together	The repeated mutual speech coordinates Babel's brickmaking; unlike the commentary's counsel toward haqq, this is a counter-example of solidarity directed toward a self-exalting project.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Gen.11.7	shared speech is confused so people cannot understand one another	The Babel scene reverses the commentary's image of people passing counsel between them: collective speech becomes unintelligible and the group is broken apart.
medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:Isa.32.17	righteousness produces peace and quiet security	Isaiah presents peace and settled confidence as the effect of righteousness; this joins ethical rightness to social calm, though it does not describe a specific dispute.
strong	tevrat	motif	Mishnah Sanhedrin 4:5	one human ancestor taught as a basis for peace among creatures	The Mishnah says humanity descends from one person so no one can claim a superior ancestry; this directly counters rival claims and grounds common human dignity in kinship.
strong	tevrat	motif	Mishnah Avot 3:2	divine presence rests where two discuss Torah	The Mishnah makes shared study a sacred meeting between people; it gives the commentary's reciprocal counsel a setting in which relationship itself matters.
strong	tevrat	motif	Babylonian Talmud, Shabbat 31a	the neighbor treated by the golden rule	Hillel summarizes Torah through the instruction not to do to another what one hates; this makes mutual regard the test for how one treats a fellow.
strong	tevrat	motif	Babylonian Talmud, Yevamot 14b	Hillel and Shammai preserve marriages despite legal disagreement	The schools disagree about rulings yet do not refuse intermarriage; this shows opposing claims coexisting without severing kinship.
strong	tevrat	motif	Babylonian Talmud, Yoma 9b	baseless hatred brings the Second Temple's destruction	The Talmud explains a communal catastrophe through hatred among people; this makes estrangement itself a source of collective loss.
medium	tevrat	yorum_gelenegi	Babylonian Talmud, Bava Metzia 30b	Jerusalem destroyed for insisting on strict law	The Talmud interprets the city's destruction as a failure to go beyond the letter of law; this provides a Jewish counter-reading in which claiming formal right without generosity cannot sustain peace.
strong	tevrat	motif	Sirach 6:14	a faithful friend is a sturdy shelter and a treasure	Ben Sira gives the close friend a protective role; this concretizes the commentary's intimate bond as refuge in human vulnerability.
medium	tevrat	motif	Sirach 6:16	a faithful friend is life-saving medicine	The friend is described as healing support found by those who fear God; this adds the companion's restorative effect to the commentary's account of connection.
strong	tevrat	motif	Sirach 28:2	forgive a neighbor before praying for forgiveness	Ben Sira makes forgiveness of another the condition mirrored in one's own prayer; this gives the commentary's repair of hostility a reciprocal religious practice.
strong	tevrat	motif	Sirach 28:8	avoid strife because anger kindles it	The sage says restraint from quarrel reduces sin and a hot-tempered person ignites conflict; this closely joins patience with the prevention of strife.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Mark.9.50	be at peace with one another after rivalry	After the disciples argue over greatness and dispute who belongs with them, Jesus tells them to have salt and be at peace with one another; the instruction answers internal rivalry directly.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Matt.7.5	correct yourself before correcting your brother	Jesus requires removing one's own plank before helping a brother with his speck; this checks mutual claims of right with self-examination before advice.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Matt.18.22	forgive a brother repeatedly	Jesus tells Peter to forgive not a few times but repeatedly; this extends the commentary's patience into sustained repair after recurring offense.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Acts.4.32	one heart and soul with possessions shared	The believers hold themselves as one community and treat possessions as common; this gives the commentary's people-joining image a material practice.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Acts.9.27	Barnabas introduces feared Saul to the apostles	When the disciples fear Saul, Barnabas stands with him and vouches for his changed life; an intermediary turns aversion into acceptance.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Rom.12.10	mutual affection and honoring one another	Paul commands familial affection and outdoing one another in honor; this is a direct ethic of reciprocal closeness.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Rom.15.7	welcome one another as Christ welcomed you	The community's welcome is grounded in the welcome it has received; this makes inclusion reciprocal rather than a claim held by one side.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:1Cor.13.4	love is patient and kind	Paul makes patience and kindness qualities of love between people; this gives the commentary's ṣabr a relational rather than solitary form.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:1Cor.13.6	love rejoices with the truth	Paul joins truth with love's response; this directly meets the commentary's shift from haqq as a contested claim to a shared good.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Eph.4.15	truth spoken in love grows the body	The letter links truth-telling to love and the growth of the whole body; this adds a communal result to the commentary's exchange of haqq.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Phil.4.2	Euodia and Syntyche urged to agree in the Lord	Paul names two women who labored in the gospel and asks them to reach agreement; the personal appeal makes counsel address an actual community conflict.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Phil.4.3	a companion asked to help the women reconcile	Paul asks a trusted coworker to assist the women who struggled beside him; the continuation makes reconciliation a shared responsibility.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:2Tim.2.24	the Lord's servant must not quarrel but be patient	The teacher is to avoid strife, remain gentle, and endure patiently; this directly links sabr to how one handles opponents.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:2Tim.2.25	correct opponents with gentleness	Correction is to be offered gently even to those who oppose; this gives mutual counsel a manner aimed at restoration rather than victory.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:1Pet.4.8	love covers many sins	Peter says sustained love covers many sins; this fits the commentary's transition from contention toward a bond that can absorb offense.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:1John.4.20	claiming love for God while hating a brother is false	The letter tests religious claim against treatment of the visible brother; this challenges any haqq claim detached from mutual care.
strong	incil	motif	Didache 14:1	reconcile with an opponent before the communal meal	The Didache bars someone at odds with a fellow from joining the Eucharist until reconciliation; this gives the commentary's peace a concrete liturgical consequence.
strong	incil	motif	1 Clement 49:4	love acts in harmony and creates no schism	Clement describes love as refusing division and doing everything in harmony; this is a Christian interpretive expansion of the bond that the commentary sees replacing estrangement.
strong	incil	motif	Gospel of Thomas 25	love and guard the brother as one's own soul	The saying treats the brother's life as one's own to protect; it gives the commentary's close-friend image an unusually intimate ethical measure.
EOF"
